title: Solitaire
blurb: Klondike, draw one or three
why: It came with Windows 3.0 in 1990.

title: Solitaire
blurb: Klondike, draw one or three
why: It came with Windows 3.0 in 1990.

title: FreeCell
blurb: Numbered deals, nearly all winnable
why: Microsoft numbered its deals. Only one of the first 32,000 cannot be won.

title: Spider
blurb: Two decks, eight runs of one suit
why: Build eight runs from king down to ace, using two decks.

title: Hearts
blurb: Four players, avoid hearts and the queen
why: A trick-taking game. The aim is to take as few points as you can.

title: Pyramid
blurb: Pairs that add to 13
why: Remove pairs that add to 13 from a pyramid of 28 cards.

title: Golf
blurb: One rank up or down, no wrapping
why: Clear seven columns of five cards before the deck runs out.

title: TriPeaks
blurb: Three peaks, wrap around, keep a streak
why: Clear three peaks of cards. Each card in a row adds to your streak.

title: Spades
blurb: Partners bid tricks, spades are trump
why: A partner game from 1930s America. Spades are always trump.

title: Euchre
blurb: 24 cards, trump, first to 10
why: A trick-taking game from the American Midwest, played with 24 cards.

title: Gin Rummy
blurb: Two players, make melds, then knock
why: A two-player rummy game from the early 1900s.

title: Cribbage
blurb: Score to 121 on a peg board
why: Said to be invented by the poet Sir John Suckling in the 1600s. It is scored with pegs on a board.

title: Crazy Eights
blurb: Match suit or rank, eights are wild
why: The game behind Uno. Every eight is wild.

title: Durak
blurb: Beat the attack, don't be left holding cards
why: Russia's best-loved card game. The last player with cards is the durak, the fool.

title: Scopa
blurb: The Italian card game, with an Italian deck
why: Italy's national card game, played with 40 cards.

title: Reversi
blurb: Flip discs to own the board
why: Invented in England in 1883. Othello is a modern version.

title: Checkers
blurb: English draughts, jumps are compulsory
why: In 2007, English draughts was proved to be a draw with perfect play.

title: Chess
blurb: The standard game, six levels
why: Its modern rules took shape in Europe around 1500.

title: Go
blurb: Surround territory on 9x9 and 13x13 boards
why: Over 2,500 years old. One of the oldest board games still played.

title: Xiangqi
blurb: Chinese chess with a river in the middle
why: China's chess, with a river across the middle of the board.

title: Shogi
blurb: Japanese chess, captured pieces can be dropped
why: Japan's chess. Captured pieces change sides and can be dropped back on the board.

title: Hex
blurb: Link your two sides, no draws
why: Invented by Piet Hein in 1942 and, separately, by John Nash in 1948.

title: Gomoku
blurb: Five in a row on a 15x15 board
why: Played with Go stones. The first to make five in a row wins.

title: Nine Men's Morris
blurb: Make mills, fly when you have three
why: An ancient game. Boards have been cut into stone since Roman times.

title: Four in a Row
blurb: Drop discs, line up four
why: Sold as Connect Four since 1974. With perfect play, the first player wins.

title: Dots and Boxes
blurb: Close boxes and move again
why: A pencil-and-paper game that the mathematician Edouard Lucas described in 1889.

title: Backgammon
blurb: Race home with an optional doubling cube
why: Its ancestors go back about 5,000 years.

title: Mancala
blurb: Oware and Kalah, sow seeds and capture
why: One of the oldest games still played. Boards are found across Africa and Asia.

title: Ludo
blurb: Roll a six to start, race home
why: From India's Pachisi. Patented in England in 1896.

title: Chinese Checkers
blurb: Hop marbles across the star
why: Not Chinese. It came from Germany in 1892 as Sternhalma.

title: Dominoes
blurb: Draw and Block games, match the ends
why: Tiles with dots. Played across Europe since the 1700s.

title: Mahjong
blurb: Match pairs of tiles, every deal can be cleared
why: This solo game matches tiles from a pile. The four-player game is different.

title: Minesweeper
blurb: Clear the board without hitting a mine
why: A Windows favourite since the early 1990s.

title: Sudoku
blurb: Fill every row, column and box
why: Named in Japan in 1984. Every puzzle here has exactly one solution.

blurb: Slide and join tiles to reach 2048
why: Written in a weekend in 2014 by Gabriele Cirulli.

title: Five Letters
blurb: Guess the word in six tries, daily or practice
why: Find the five-letter word in six tries.

title: Wiki Race
blurb: Reach one article from another using links only
why: Players race between Wikipedia articles using only links. Here it uses your Wikipedia.

title: Letter by Letter
blurb: Guess the word letter by letter from your Wiktionary
why: Keep the balloon up by guessing the letters of a word.

title: Quizzical
blurb: Questions made from your Wikipedia
why: Questions made from the articles in your Wikipedia.

title: Jigsaw
blurb: A picture from your Wikipedia, cut into pieces
why: Jigsaw puzzles began in the 1760s as maps cut into pieces to teach geography.

title: Snake
blurb: Eat to grow and go faster. Walls or wrap-around.
why: Based on the 1976 arcade game Blockade. On Nokia phones from 1997.

title: Bricks
blurb: Paddle and ball against a wall of bricks
why: Based on Atari's Breakout of 1976.

title: Fifteen
blurb: Slide the tiles into order
why: The 15 puzzle craze swept America and Europe in 1880.

title: Same Game
blurb: Clear blocks of the same colour
why: Invented in 1985 by Kuniaki Moribe as Chain Shot.

title: Pegs
blurb: Jump pegs over pegs until one is left
why: Peg solitaire, a game for one player. It dates back to at least 17th-century France.

title: Pattern
blurb: Use the row and column clues to reveal a picture
why: Nonograms, a picture puzzle that became popular in Japan in the late 1980s.

title: Slant
blurb: Draw diagonal lines, each number counting those touching it
why: Known in Japan as Gokigen Naname.

title: Light Up
blurb: Place lamps to light every square, none lighting another
why: Known in Japan as Akari.

title: Loopy
blurb: Draw one loop that uses the right sides of each number
why: Known in Japan as Slitherlink.

title: Bridges
blurb: Join the islands with the bridges each number asks for
why: Known in Japan as Hashiwokakero.

title: Galaxies
blurb: Split the grid into regions that look the same upside down
why: Known in Japan as Tentaisho, meaning heavenly bodies.

title: Rectangles
blurb: Divide the grid into rectangles of the numbered areas
why: Known in Japan as Shikaku, meaning square.

title: Keen
blurb: Fill the grid so each cage makes its number
why: Like KenKen, invented in 2004 by Tetsuya Miyamoto.

title: Unequal
blurb: Fill the grid, obeying the greater-than and less-than signs
why: Known as Futoshiki, Japanese for inequality.

title: Pearl
blurb: Draw a loop through the pearls as shown
why: Known in Japan as Masyu.

title: Range
blurb: Shade squares so each number sees the right count
why: Known in Japan as Kuromasu.

title: Singles
blurb: Shade repeated numbers, with no shaded squares touching
why: Known in Japan as Hitori, meaning alone.

title: Filling
blurb: Fill in numbers so each region's size matches its number
why: Known in Japan as Fillomino.

title: Black Box
blurb: Fire beams in to find the hidden balls
why: Created by the games designer Eric Solomon in the 1970s.

title: Flip
blurb: Light every square by flipping groups of squares
why: Related to Lights Out.

title: Unruly
blurb: Fill with two colours: balanced lines, no three in a row
why: Also called Binairo or Takuzu.

title: Yacht
blurb: Five dice, 13 rows. Play alone or against computers.
why: A public-domain dice game. It later became Yahtzee.

title: Liar's Dice
blurb: Bid, bluff and call. 2 to 6 players.
why: A bluffing game with dice under cups. Played in South America as Perudo.

title: Fleet
blurb: Hide your ships, find the computer's
why: Finding hidden ships on a grid began as a pencil-and-paper game before the First World War.

title: Code Breaker
blurb: Crack a hidden code from the clues
why: Guessing a hidden code from clues goes back to the paper game Bulls and Cows.

title: Code Breaker
blurb: Crack a hidden code from the clues
why: Guessing a hidden code from clues goes back to the paper game Bulls and Cows.

title: Pinball
blurb: Flippers, bumpers, lanes and multiball
why: Flippers arrived in 1947. Before that, pinball was mostly luck.

title: Rocks
blurb: Turn, thrust and shoot rocks that split
why: Every rock you hit splits into smaller rocks.

title: Last Line
blurb: Drones march down and shields wear away
why: Rows of invaders moving down the screen made this kind of shooter popular in 1978.

title: Lander
blurb: Land softly on a pad before the fuel runs out
why: Land gently with the fuel you have, as Apollo crews did on the Moon.

title: Paddles
blurb: Two-paddle tennis against the computer or a friend
why: Two paddles and a ball. It started the video game industry in 1972.

title: Memory
blurb: Match the pairs of pictures
why: A game of turning over cards to find pairs. Children play it everywhere.

title: Echo
blurb: Repeat the growing sequence of pads
why: Repeat the growing sequence of colours and tones.

title: Tic-Tac-Toe
blurb: Three in a row, against the computer or a friend
why: Played perfectly, tic-tac-toe is always a draw.

title: Koi-Koi
blurb: Hanafuda flower cards, make yaku, call koi-koi
why: Hanafuda are Japan's flower cards. They began when Western playing cards were banned in the 1600s.

title: Truco
blurb: Argentine bluffing game, envido, play to 15 or 30
why: The bluffing card game of Argentina and Uruguay, played with a Spanish deck.

title: Belote
blurb: Partners, trump, belote and rebelote
why: France's most played card game. Partners bid for trump.

title: Skat
blurb: Three players, bid, take the skat, name a game
why: Germany's national card game, invented in Altenburg around 1810.

title: Teen Patti
blurb: Blind or seen, side show, play with chips
why: India's three-card game. It is like three-card brag.

title: Bridge
blurb: Bid, play and defend with a computer partner
why: Contract bridge took its modern form with Harold Vanderbilt in 1925.

title: Texas Hold’em
blurb: Chips, blinds, all-in and side pots
why: Played for chips only.

title: Blackjack
blurb: Closer to 21 than the dealer, split and double
why: Twenty-one against the dealer. A strategy hint is optional.

title: Canasta
blurb: Meld cards, freeze the pile, play to 5000
why: Canasta came from Uruguay in the 1940s and spread worldwide within ten years.

title: Big Two
blurb: Beat the last play, twos are high
why: A climbing game played across southern China and Taiwan.

title: Tien Len
blurb: Runs, pairs in a row and chops
why: Vietnam's national card game, where the two is the highest card.

title: Janggi
blurb: Korean chess with palaces and cannons
why: Korean chess. The generals stay in their palaces. Cannons must jump over one piece.

title: Makruk
blurb: Thai chess, slower than chess
why: Thai chess, close to the Indian game that chess grew from.

title: International Draughts
blurb: 10x10 with flying kings, take the most pieces
why: International draughts is played on a 10 by 10 board across Europe and Africa.

title: Hnefatafl
blurb: Copenhagen rules, the king runs for a corner
why: The Viking board game. The king escapes to a corner or is captured.

title: Hnefatafl
blurb: Copenhagen rules, the king runs for a corner
why: The Viking board game. The king escapes to a corner or is captured.

title: Royal Game of Ur
blurb: A race game 4,500 years old, four dice
why: Played in Mesopotamia 4,500 years ago. Its rules survive on a clay tablet.

title: Snakes and Ladders
blurb: Race to square 100, up ladders and down snakes
why: Snakes and Ladders began in India as Moksha Patam, a game about good and bad deeds.

title: Carrom
blurb: Flick the striker, pocket coins, cover the queen
why: Flick and pocket on a wooden board. Played in homes across South Asia.

title: Mahjong for Four
blurb: Hong Kong style against computers
why: The four-player tile game played across China and beyond.

title: Circuit
blurb: Four tracks, rival cars and a ghost of your best lap
why: Atari's Gran Trak 10 put a wheel and pedals on an arcade machine in 1974.

title: Road Rush
blurb: Hills, curves and traffic against the clock
why: 1980s arcade racers made a 3D road by scaling flat strips.

title: Hopper
blurb: Run, jump and stomp through six short levels
why: In platform games, jumping between ledges is the whole game.

title: Muncher
blurb: Eat every dot while four chasers follow you
why: Maze chase games were common in arcades by 1980. Each chaser moves in its own way.

title: Crossing
blurb: Hop across roads and rivers
why: A 1981 arcade game about getting across a road.

title: Blast
blurb: Drop bombs, break blocks and set off chains
why: Bombs that blast in four directions and set each other off started a whole kind of game.

title: Quest
blurb: A small adventure: find a sword, then beat the boss
why: A sword, a key and a locked door. Top-down adventures have used these since the early 1980s.

title: ZimiKart
blurb: Eight racers, six tracks, drift for a boost
why: Kart games make a 3D road by tilting one flat picture of the track. 1990s consoles did this in hardware.

title: Chess Puzzles
blurb: 15,000 rated Lichess puzzles, your own rating
why: Lichess rates each puzzle by how many players solved it. All puzzles are open data.

title: Opening Trainer
blurb: 3,800 named openings, play your side
why: Chess players have named opening moves for generations. ECO codes run from A00 to E99.

title: Go Problems
blurb: Make a group live, or kill it
why: Tsumego are Go's life-and-death problems. They teach you to plan moves ahead.

title: Sokoban
blurb: Push the crates onto the rings
why: Sokoban is Japanese for warehouse keeper. Thinking Rabbit published it in 1982.

title: First Lines
blurb: Name the book from its first line
why: Old books were once known by their first words, called the incipit. Here you name a book from its opening line, read from your Gutenberg library.

title: Flags
blurb: Name the country from its flag
why: National flags in their modern form date from the late 1700s. Here you name countries from the flags in your Wikipedia.

title: Higher or Lower
blurb: Compare places and things from your Wikipedia
why: Guessing whether the next number is higher or lower is an old card game. Here you compare people, areas, heights and river lengths from your Wikipedia.

title: Timeline
blurb: Put events from your Wikipedia in order
why: Timelines that put events in order were drawn by Joseph Priestley in the 1760s. Here you rebuild one from the events of your Wikipedia.

title: Spelling Bee
blurb: Words from seven letters, checked in your Wiktionary
why: Spelling bees began in the United States in the 1800s. Here you make words from seven letters, and your Wiktionary decides which are words.

title: Mini Crossword
blurb: A small crossword clued by your Wiktionary
why: The first newspaper crossword ran in New York in 1913. This small one takes its clues from the definitions in your Wiktionary.

title: Telephone
blurb: Write a clue; your friend finds the article
why: Telephone, or Chinese whispers, passes a message along and it changes on the way. Here the message is a clue, and the library holds the answer.

title: Dictionary Bluff
blurb: Fake meanings for real rare words, passed round
why: Balderdash and Fictionary are games of invented definitions. Here the real words and meanings come from your own Wiktionary.

title: Babel
blurb: One word in five languages: name it in English
why: The story of the Tower of Babel explains why people speak many languages. Many words still show that languages share ancestors.

title: Sky Detective
blurb: Name what is in tonight’s real sky
why: Stargazers have named the bright stars and planets for thousands of years. This game works out the real sky for your place and time.

title: Drop Pin
blurb: Pin a place on your own offline map
why: Finding a place on a map became a popular game in 2013. Here the map can be your own offline one.

title: Stacker
blurb: Fit falling pieces into rows. Hold a piece and see where it will land.
why: Falling-block stacking began with Tetris, written in Moscow in 1984.

title: Untangle
blurb: Drag the points until no lines cross
why: Based on Planarity, a graph puzzle from 2005.

title: Map
blurb: Colour the map in four colours, no neighbours alike
why: The four colour problem was posed in 1852 and settled by computer in 1976.

title: Group
blurb: Fill a grid so it follows a group table
why: Group tables are named for Arthur Cayley, who set them out in 1854.

title: Sixteen
blurb: Slide whole rows and columns to sort the grid
why: A cousin of the 15 puzzle, which swept America and Europe in 1880.

title: Net
blurb: Turn the tiles until the network joins up
why: Based on NetWalk, a puzzle video game from 1996.

title: Cube
blurb: Roll a cube over the grid to pick up blue squares
why: Based on a Java web game by Paul Scott.

title: Dominosa
blurb: Tile the grid so every number pair is used once
why: Widely credited to O. S. Adler, whose initials gave it part of its name.

title: Flood
blurb: Flood the grid with one colour in few moves
why: Based on a web game called Flood-It.

title: Inertia
blurb: Slide around collecting gems, and avoid the mines
why: Originally written for Windows by Ben Olmstead.

title: Magnets
blurb: Place magnets so every line has the right poles
why: Credited to the puzzle site Janko, and added to the collection by James Harvey.

title: Mosaic
blurb: Each number counts the shaded squares around it
why: Also known as Fill-a-Pix.

title: Netslide
blurb: Slide rows and columns to join up the network
why: Joins the networks of Net to the sliding rows of Sixteen.

title: Palisade
blurb: Draw walls to make regions of the right size
why: Based on Five Cells, a puzzle from the Japanese publisher Nikoli.

title: Signpost
blurb: Link the squares in order by following the arrows
why: Credited to the puzzle site Janko, which calls it Pfeilpfad, arrow path.

title: Tents
blurb: Pitch a tent by every tree, with no tents touching
why: A tree-and-tent pencil puzzle found on many websites.

title: Towers
blurb: Build towers; each clue counts those you can see
why: Also known as Skyscrapers.

title: Tracks
blurb: Lay a railway from one end to the other
why: Added to the collection by James Harvey.

title: Twiddle
blurb: Turn blocks of tiles to sort the grid
why: Generalises a door puzzle from the game Metroid Prime 2.

title: Undead
blurb: Place ghosts, vampires and zombies by what mirrors show
why: Invented by David Millar as Haunted Mirror Maze.
